claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3-type chemistry is an example of the proposed coating composition.
FCC/BCC interfaces in the coating have a lattice-parameter and elastic mismatch.
The mismatch at FCC/BCC interfaces produces elastic strain fields.
Elastic strain fields at FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Interface-mediated obstruction of dislocations increases the activation energy for creep deformation.
Increasing the activation energy for creep reduces the steady-state creep rate under sustained high-temperature loading.
The dual-phase coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate than a homogenized single-phase coating.
The dual-phase coating will develop a plateau in creep strain relative to the single-phase baseline.
Dislocation pile-up will be observable at FCC/BCC interfaces by high-resolution microscopy.
A single-phase coating lacking engineered FCC/BCC interfaces will exhibit higher creep rates than the dual-phase coating.
A single-phase coating lacking engineered FCC/BCC interfaces will exhibit less effective dislocation pinning.
The interface-controlled mechanism will dominate at 800–900 °C under sustained stress below the yield threshold of both phases.
The interface-controlled mechanism may cease to dominate at ultrahigh stress.
Extraneous microstructural defects may confound the inferred effect of FCC/BCC interfaces on creep.

contradictions.description: The intervention states that interface characteristics are the only variable, but comparing a dual-phase FCC/BCC coating with a single-phase coating necessarily also changes phase constitution and potentially phase fractions, grain structure, and properties created by the homogenization or spraying treatment.
